say: Your microwave boils soup in two minutes, but the plate and the walls barely get warm. So where's all that heat coming from?
Inside hides a gadget called a magnetron. It fires invisible waves that flip back and forth billions of times a second.
Your food is full of water, and each water molecule is lopsided: one end slightly plus, one end slightly minus.
Every flip yanks those molecules around. They spin, crash into their neighbors, and all that chaos becomes heat.
Glass and ceramic give the waves almost nothing to grab, so they zoom right through. The plate mostly gets warm from the food.
Metal walls bounce the waves like mirrors. The door's metal screen has holes too tiny for the waves, but light gets out.
Bouncing waves pile up in some places and cancel out in others. Hot spots, cold spots. That's why the plate spins.
And no, it doesn't cook from the inside out. The waves reach only about a centimeter in, and the middle heats the slow way.
Fun fact: in the nineteen forties, Percy Spencer stood near a radar magnetron, and the candy bar in his pocket melted.
So your food basically heats itself! Follow Simply Weird for more weird stuff like this.
